mainTopic: The story of אליעזר זעירא and assessment בששים; רבי שמעון on ripe produce and רב's rulings; the משנה of stacking in a friend's field; and the משנה of sending fire through a חרש, שוטה, or קטן.
overview: The amud opens with a story. אליעזר זעירא is jailed by the officials of the ריש גלותא for publicly mourning ירושלים. He proves he is a scholar with a question about cutting a young date cluster, which is assessed בששים, and שמואל confirms the answer. The גמרא then explains רבי שמעון's view that fully ripe produce is paid at its actual value, because it no longer needs the field. It reports that רב ruled the הלכה like רבי שמעון, and that in a separate case about a wife's כתובה he judged like רבי מאיר. A new משנה follows about stacking grain in a friend's field with and without permission. רב פפא shows that this משנה fits רבי by explaining that it is talking about a threshing-floor guard. Another new משנה deals with fire handed to a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, or passed between several people, and decides who is liable. The גמרא begins a dispute about it: ריש לקיש says the giver is liable for handing over a flame, while רבי יוחנן exempts him until he hands over branches, and that statement continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Wearing black shoes in the market
steps.stepSummary: אליעזר זעירא stands in the market of נהרדעא wearing black shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was wearing black shoes and standing in the market of נהרדעא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the scene for a story. A man is standing in public wearing black shoes, which stands out. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man is אליעזר זעירא, who was named just before this line. Wearing black shoes was unusual, so people would notice. That is what starts the whole incident.

keyTerms.meaning: נהרדעא, a major Jewish city in בבל

phrases.english: He was wearing black shoes,
and standing in the market of נהרדעא.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Story setup: a man publicly wears black shoes in נהרדעא.

steps.title: The officials ask why he wears these shoes
steps.stepSummary: Officials of the ריש גלותא find him and ask what is special about his shoes.
steps.simpleTranslation: People of the ריש גלותא's household found him and said to him: What is different about these shoes?
steps.whatsHappening: The officials of the ריש גלותא notice the unusual shoes and ask him to explain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a real question. They want to know why he is dressing differently from everyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: the Exilarch, the official leader of the Jews in בבל

phrases.english: People of the house of the ריש גלותא found him

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: מַאי שְׁנָא הָנֵי מְסָאנֵי?
phrases.english: and said to him: What is different about these shoes?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why he is wearing unusual black shoes.

steps.title: He is mourning for ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: He explains that he wears them because he is mourning over ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Because I am mourning over ירושלים.
steps.whatsHappening: He answers that the black shoes are a sign of mourning for the destruction of ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Black clothing was a sign of mourning. He is presenting his act as a public expression of grief over the חורבן.

phrases.english: He said to them: Because I am mourning over ירושלים.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The shoes are a sign of mourning for ירושלים.

steps.title: They think he is showing off and jail him
steps.stepSummary: They challenge whether he is important enough for this, assume it is arrogance, and imprison him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Are you so important that you mourn over ירושלים? They thought it was arrogance, so they brought him and locked him up.
steps.whatsHappening: The officials reject his explanation. They decide he is acting arrogantly and put him in jail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their objection is not to mourning itself. They object to an ordinary person making a public show that seems fit only for someone important. They see it as יוהרא, showing off.

phrases.english: They said to him: Are you so important
to mourn over ירושלים?
They thought it was arrogance,
so they brought him and imprisoned him.

steps.kashyaTarget: His claim that he is mourning for ירושלים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only an important person may make such a public display; for anyone else it is arrogance.

steps.title: He claims to be a great scholar
steps.stepSummary: He replies that he is a great man, so his mourning is appropriate.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I am a great man.
steps.whatsHappening: He answers their charge of arrogance. He says he really is a great Torah scholar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their complaint was that he was not important enough. He answers that he is important, so the public mourning suits him.

keyTerms.meaning: a great man, a Torah scholar

phrases.english: He said to them: I am a great man.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual rebuttal: he is in fact a scholar.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He is an ordinary person showing off.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is a scholar, so his mourning is fitting.

steps.title: How do we know?
steps.stepSummary: They ask how they can know he is a scholar.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: How do we know?
steps.whatsHappening: The officials ask for proof that he really is a great scholar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying it is not enough. They want evidence, and that sets up the test that follows.

phrases.english: They said to him: How do we know?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Proof that he is a scholar.

steps.title: He offers a test of Torah knowledge
steps.stepSummary: He offers that either they ask him a question or he asks them. They tell him to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Either you ask me something, or I will ask you something. They said to him: You ask.
steps.whatsHappening: He proposes to prove his greatness with a halachic question. They choose to let him ask. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof will come through learning. If he asks a question they cannot answer and he can, that shows he is a scholar.

keyTerms.meaning: a matter (here, a question of הלכה)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אוֹ אַתּוּן בְּעוֹ מִינַּאי מִילְּתָא,
phrases.english: He said to them: Either you ask me a matter,
or I will ask you a matter.
They said to him: You ask.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He will prove himself by asking a halachic question.

steps.title: What does one pay for cutting a young date cluster?
steps.stepSummary: He asks what someone pays if he cuts off another person's young date cluster.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Someone who cuts a young date cluster, what does he pay?
steps.whatsHappening: Now comes the test question. If someone cuts down another person's young, unripe date cluster, how much must he pay?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is hard because the cluster is worth little now but would have become valuable dates. The question is which value the payment should be based on.

keyTerms.meaning: a young, unripe date cluster or shoot

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: הַאי מַאן דְּקַץ כּוּפְרָא,
phrases.english: He said to them: One who cuts a young date cluster,
what does he pay?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי מַאן דְּקַץ כּוּפְרָא מַאי מְשַׁלֵּם
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to value damage done to unripe produce.

steps.title: First answer: pay for the young cluster
steps.stepSummary: They answer that he pays the value of the young cluster.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: He pays the value of the young cluster.
steps.whatsHappening: The officials give a simple answer: pay what the unripe cluster is worth right now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer looks only at the cluster's current value. It ignores what the cluster would have grown into.

keyTerms.meaning: the value of, the price of

phrases.english: They said to him: He pays the value of the young cluster.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Pay the current value of the unripe cluster.

steps.title: But they would have become dates!
steps.stepSummary: He objects that the cluster would have grown into valuable dates.
steps.simpleTranslation: But they would have become dates!
steps.whatsHappening: אליעזר זעירא attacks their answer. The owner lost more than a little cluster, because it would have become full dates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Paying only the cluster's current value shortchanges the owner. The owner lost the future dates too.

phrases.english: But they would have become dates!

steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that he pays the cluster's current value
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner lost the future dates, not just the cluster, so that payment is too low.

steps.title: Second answer: pay for the dates
steps.stepSummary: They change their answer: he pays the value of the dates.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: He pays the value of the dates.
steps.whatsHappening: The officials switch to the opposite extreme. He should pay the full value of ripe dates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This fixes the problem of paying too little. But it now charges the damager for something that did not exist yet.

phrases.english: They said to him: He pays the value of the dates.

steps.terutzMaskana: Pay for the full ripe dates.

steps.title: But he did not take dates from him!
steps.stepSummary: He objects that the damager never took ripe dates.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: But he did not take dates from him!
steps.whatsHappening: He attacks the second answer too. The damager only cut an unripe cluster; he never took ripe dates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dates might never have ripened, and growing them would still have needed time on the tree. So charging the full price of dates is too much. Both of their answers fail.
steps.whatToRemember: Both easy answers fail: paying for the cluster alone is too little, and paying for ripe dates is too much. A middle method is needed.

phrases.english: He said to them: But it was not dates
that he took from him!

steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that he pays the value of the dates
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He took only an unripe cluster, not ripe dates, so full date value is too much.

steps.title: They ask him for the answer
steps.stepSummary: Stuck, they ask him to tell them the answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: You tell us.
steps.whatsHappening: The officials give up and ask אליעזר זעירא for the correct answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They have no more answers. That already partly proves his point that he knows more than they do.

phrases.english: They said to him: You tell us.

steps.sheelahInformationSought: The correct method of valuing the damage.

steps.title: The answer: assess it בששים
steps.stepSummary: He answers that the damage is assessed as part of an area sixty times larger.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: It is assessed in sixty.
steps.whatsHappening: He gives the correct rule: the damage is valued בששים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of valuing the cluster alone or as ripe dates, we look at how much a piece of land sixty times larger drops in value because of this loss. This is a middle path between the two failed answers. It follows the same idea as the משנה's rule for a damaged field: the loss is judged as part of a larger area, not on its own.

keyTerms.meaning: in sixty; assessed as part of an area sixty times larger

steps.confusionAlert: בששים here has nothing to do with ביטול בששים in כשרות. It is a way of assessing damages, not a rule about mixtures.

phrases.english: He said to them: In sixty.
phrases.notes: He means: see how much a plot sixty times larger loses in value because of this damage.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The damage is assessed relative to an area sixty times larger.
steps.whyThisMatters: This connects the story to the main halachic topic here: the בששים method of assessing damage to produce that is not yet ripe.

steps.title: Who agrees with you?
steps.stepSummary: They ask who supports his ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Who says like you?
steps.whatsHappening: The officials want an authority who backs up his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They do not simply accept his word. They need confirmation before admitting he is a scholar.

phrases.english: They said to him: Who says like you?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: An authority who confirms his ruling.

steps.title: Ask שמואל
steps.stepSummary: He tells them שמואל is alive and his court is active, so they can ask him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: שמואל is alive and his court is standing.
steps.whatsHappening: He points them to שמואל, the leading sage of נהרדעא, to check his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He is confident enough to let a living authority judge his ruling. That is the final step of his proof.

keyTerms.meaning: שמואל, the great אמורא of נהרדעא

phrases.english: He said to them: Here, שמואל is alive
and his court exists.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא שְׁמוּאֵל חַי וּבֵית דִּינוֹ קַיָּים

steps.title: שמואל confirms and they release him
steps.stepSummary: They send the question to שמואל, who says the answer of בששים is correct, and they free him.
steps.simpleTranslation: They sent it before שמואל. He said to them: He is telling you correctly, in sixty. And they released him.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל confirms that בששים is the right answer. The officials then let אליעזר זעירא go.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's approval proves two things at once: the halacha is בששים, and אליעזר זעירא really is a great scholar. Since he is a scholar, his public mourning was not arrogance, so they free him.

keyTerms.meaning: he is saying well, he is correct

steps.whatToRemember: Damage to unripe produce is assessed בששים, confirmed by שמואל. The story also shows that a true scholar may publicly mourn for ירושלים.

phrases.english: They sent before שמואל,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לְהוּ: שַׁפִּיר קָאָמַר לְכוּ בְּשִׁשִּׁים,
phrases.english: he said to them: He is telling you correctly, in sixty,
and they released him.

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The assessment is בששים, and אליעזר זעירא is shown to be a scholar and released.

steps.title: What is רבי שמעון's reason for paying full value on ripe produce?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי שמעון from the משנה and asks for the reason behind his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: if the animal ate fully ripe produce, and so on. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back a line from the משנה, where רבי שמעון says ripe produce is paid in full. It asks why he holds this, setting up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now, the damage was assessed as part of a larger area (בששים). רבי שמעון says that for fully ripe fruit, the owner pays the actual value. The גמרא wants to know why ripe fruit is different.

keyTerms.meaning: Fully ripe produce, ready to be picked
Etc.; the rest of the quote is in the משנה

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
If it ate fully ripe produce, etc.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from our משנה. 'It' is the animal that went into someone else's field.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the story ending in step 17, the גמרא moves on to the next opinion in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source or logic for רבי שמעון's rule that fully ripe produce is paid at full value.

steps.title: Ripe produce no longer needs the field, so it is paid as is
steps.stepSummary: The rule of assessing damage as part of a field applies only to produce that still needs the field. Ripe produce does not, so it is paid at its actual value.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Torah says 'and it feeds in another's field.' This teaches that we assess the damage as part of the field. But that only applies to things that still need the field. These ripe fruits do not need the field anymore, so the owner must pay for them as they are.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why רבי שמעון makes the owner pay full value for ripe produce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'בשדה אחר' is the source for assessing damage as part of a field. רבי שמעון reads it as covering only produce still growing and depending on the field. Fully ripe fruit is basically finished, so it is no longer part of the field and is paid at its own value.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And it feeds in another's field': the פסוק about an animal grazing in someone else's field
We assess the damage as part of the whole field
This applies only to…; limits a rule
As they are; at their actual value

phrases.english: That which the Merciful One said
"And it feeds in another's field"
teaches that we assess the damage as part of the field,
this applies only to something that needs the field;
these, since they do not need the field,
he must pay for them as they are.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק's rule of assessing the damage as part of a field covers only produce that still needs the field. Ripe produce does not need it, so it is paid at full value.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the 'sixty times' method is not a blanket rule. It depends on whether the produce is still part of the field.

steps.title: רב judged like רבי מאיר and ruled the הלכה like רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר חייא reports in the name of רבי ירמיה בר אבא that רב judged a case like רבי מאיר and ruled the הלכה like רבי שמעון.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר חייא said in the name of רבי ירמיה בר אבא: רב judged a case like רבי מאיר, and he ruled the הלכה like רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement reports two rulings of רב. The next two steps explain each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two different kinds of rulings here. 'דן' means רב decided an actual case brought before him. 'פסק הלכתא' means he stated the official rule. The גמרא does not yet say which cases these were.

keyTerms.meaning: Ruled the הלכה; stated the official rule
A תנא whose opinion רב followed in one case

phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Chiyya said
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba said:
Rav judged like Rabbi Meir,
and ruled the halacha like Rabbi Shimon.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר חִיָּיא אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Since רבי שמעון's view was just explained, the גמרא brings a statement about how רב ruled.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב decided an actual case like רבי מאיר and ruled the הלכה like רבי שמעון.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'דן' and 'פסק הלכתא' as the same thing. One is deciding an actual case; the other is declaring the rule.

steps.title: The case where רב judged like רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא identifies the case: a wife who signed the second sale of a field her כתובה was secured on. רבי מאיר says she loses her claim; רבי יהודה says she can say she only did it to please her husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'רב judged like רבי מאיר,' as it is taught: If a husband wrote a sale document to a first buyer and she did not sign for him, then to a second buyer and she did sign, she has lost her כתובה, according to רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says she can say: 'I did it to please my husband. What claim do you have against me?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the first half of רב's statement by bringing the ברייתא where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה argue. רב followed רבי מאיר there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds that her signature on the second sale counts, so she gives up her right to collect from that field. רבי יהודה says she can claim she signed only to keep peace with her husband and never meant to give up her rights. רב decided like רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא
Her כתובה; the money owed to her, secured on her husband's property
The תנא who argues with רבי מאיר here

phrases.english: Rav judged like Rabbi Meir, as it is taught:
If he wrote a sale document to the first buyer and she did not sign for him,
phrases.notes: The husband is selling a field that his wife's כתובה is secured on, and 'she' is the wife.

phrases.english: then to the second buyer, and she signed for him,
she has lost her ketubah; these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר, יְכוֹלָה הִיא שֶׁתֹּאמַר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: she can say:
"I did it to please my husband;
what claim do you have against me?"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first part of רב's statement from step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the case of the wife who signed the second sale, רב followed רבי מאיר: she loses her claim on that field.

steps.title: רב ruled like רבי שמעון: ripe produce is paid in full
steps.stepSummary: The second half of רב's statement refers to our משנה. רב ruled like רבי שמעון that ripe produce is paid at its full value, measure for measure.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he ruled the הלכה like רבי שמעון,' as we learned in the משנה: רבי שמעון says, if it ate fully ripe produce, he pays for fully ripe produce. If a סאה, a סאה; if two סאה, two סאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second half of רב's statement. It points back to our משנה: רב ruled like רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ties the section together. רבי שמעון's view, which step 19 explained, is the accepted הלכה according to רב. The owner pays exactly for the amount eaten: one סאה for one סאה, two for two.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה
Pays; the owner pays for what the animal ate
A measure of volume for grain or produce

phrases.english: And he ruled the halacha like Rabbi Shimon,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דִּתְנַן, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: as we learned in the mishna: Rabbi Shimon says:
If it ate fully ripe produce,
it pays for fully ripe produce;

phrases.aramaic: אִם סְאָה – סְאָה, אִם סָאתַיִם – סָאתַיִם.
phrases.english: if a se'ah, a se'ah; if two se'ahs, two se'ahs.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְסַק הִלְכְתָא כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן – כִּי הָא דִּתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of רב's statement from step 20 and brings us back to our משנה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to רב, the הלכה follows רבי שמעון: if an animal eats fully ripe produce, the owner pays its full value, measure for measure.
steps.whatToRemember: Ripe produce no longer needs the field, so it is not assessed as part of a larger area. רב ruled like רבי שמעון that it is paid in full: a סאה for a סאה.

steps.title: Stacking grain in a friend's field
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules on someone who stacks his produce in another person's field. Without permission, the field owner is not liable if his animal eats it, and the stack owner is liable if the animal gets hurt. With permission, the field owner is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone piles his grain in his friend's field without asking, and the field owner's animal eats it, the field owner is exempt. If the animal gets hurt from the grain, the grain owner pays. If he piled it there with permission, the field owner pays for damage to the grain.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It deals with grain stacked in someone else's field, with and without permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without permission, the grain owner is treated as an intruder. The field owner has no duty to protect the grain, and the grain owner must pay if his pile hurts the field owner's animal. Once permission is given, the field owner takes on responsibility for the grain.

keyTerms.meaning: One who piles up produce into a stack
A stack or pile of grain

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who stacks [his produce] inside his fellow's field
without permission,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲכָלָתַן בְּהֶמְתּוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַשָּׂדֶה – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and the animal of the field's owner ate them – [the field owner] is exempt.
And if [the animal] was injured by them –
the owner of the stack is liable.
But if he stacked with permission –
the owner of the field is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the previous discussion ended with רב's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without permission, the field owner is exempt and the stack owner is liable for injury to the animal. With permission, the field owner is liable for damage to the stack.

steps.title: Does the משנה go against רבי?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the משנה disagrees with רבי. רבי holds that a homeowner is responsible only if he explicitly accepts the job of guarding, and the משנה makes the field owner liable from permission alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say our משנה does not follow רבי? If it followed רבי, there would be a problem, because רבי says the homeowner is not responsible until he takes on the job of guarding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the end of the משנה. It seems to clash with רבי's view, which requires the owner to clearly agree to guard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that permission alone makes the field owner liable. רבי holds that permission to bring things in is not enough; the owner must accept the job of guarding. So the משנה appears to follow the other view and not רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? (suggests a possibly unwanted conclusion)
He accepts upon himself to guard

phrases.english: GEMARA: Shall we say that we learned [the משנה] not in line with Rabbi?
For if it were like Rabbi – doesn't he say:

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיְּקַבֵּל עָלָיו בַּעַל הַבַּיִת לִשְׁמוֹר!
phrases.english: [He is not liable] until the homeowner accepts upon himself to guard!
phrases.notes: This is רבי's view in an earlier משנה about bringing things into someone's courtyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the last ruling of the משנה in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the field owner is liable just because he gave permission.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי requires explicit acceptance of guarding, so a ruling based on permission alone seems to contradict him.

steps.title: רב פפא: the case of a threshing-floor guard
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the משנה is talking about a professional guard of threshing floors. When he says 'come in and stack,' it means 'come in and I will guard it for you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Here we are talking about the guard of the threshing floors. Since he told him 'come in and stack,' it is the same as saying 'come in and I will guard it for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא defends the משנה. He shows that it can fit רבי after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא shows the משנה can fit רבי's rule that guarding must be accepted. For a person whose job is guarding, giving permission already counts as accepting the job. So the משנה is a case of acceptance, and it does not disagree with רבי.

keyTerms.meaning: The guard of the threshing floors

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה fits רבי. The field owner is a professional guard, so his permission already means he accepted guarding.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Here we are dealing with the guard of the threshing floors,
since he said to him: "Come in and stack" –
it is [as if he said]: "Come in and I will guard for you."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: הָכָא – בְּנָטַר בֵּי דָרֵי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 24 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) to a professional guard.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to make any field owner liable from permission alone, against רבי.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a threshing-floor guard, whose permission counts as accepting guarding, so it fits רבי.

steps.title: Sending fire through someone else
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: if someone hands fire to a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, he is exempt in human court but liable to Heaven. If he hands it to a פקח, the פקח is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sends fire in the hand of a חרש, שוטה, or קטן is exempt by human law but liable by the law of Heaven. If he sent it with a פקח, the פקח is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins about fire damage done through another person. It asks who is responsible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חרש, שוטה, or קטן is not legally responsible. The sender is also not liable in court, since he did not do the damage directly, but Heaven holds him responsible. A פקח is responsible for his own actions, so the liability moves fully to him.

keyTerms.meaning: A deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor: people not legally responsible

steps.confusionAlert: 'Exempt' here only means a human court cannot make him pay. He still did wrong and is liable before Heaven.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who sends the fire
in the hand of a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor –
is exempt by human laws,
but liable by the laws of Heaven.
If he sent it in the hand of a competent person –
the competent person is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַשּׁוֹלֵחַ אֶת הַבְּעֵרָה בְּיַד חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה on a new topic, fire damage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sending fire through a חרש, שוטה, or קטן: exempt in court, liable to Heaven. Through a פקח: the פקח is liable.

steps.title: Fire and wood brought by two people
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues: when one person brings fire and another brings wood, the one who brought the wood is liable. When one brings wood and another brings fire, the one who brought the fire is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If one brought the fire and another brought the wood, the one who brought the wood is liable. If one brought the wood and another brought the fire, the one who brought the fire is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with two people who each add part of a dangerous fire. It rules on who pays.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both orders, the second person is liable. He is the one whose action turned the setup into a dangerous, spreading fire. The first person's part alone was not yet the cause of the damage.
steps.whatToRemember: The person whose action completes the fire, whoever came last, is the one liable.

phrases.english: If one brought the fire
and one [other person] brought the wood –
the one who brought the wood is liable.
If one brought the wood
and one [other person] brought the fire –
the one who brought the fire is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶחָד הֵבִיא אֶת הָאוּר וְאֶחָד הֵבִיא אֶת הָעֵצִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה about fire with a case of two people acting together.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The second person, whose action completes the dangerous fire, is liable.

steps.title: Someone else fans the fire, or the wind does
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends its fire cases. If another person fans the fire, the fanner is liable. If the wind fans it, nobody is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: If another person came and fanned the fire, the one who fanned it is liable. If the wind fanned it, all of them are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds two more cases to its list. It covers what happens when someone else, or the wind, makes the fire grow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability goes to the last person whose action actually made the fire spread. If a person fanned it, he is the direct cause and he pays. If only the wind did it, no person caused the damage, so the one who brought the fire and the one who brought the wood are both exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Fanned the fire (made it flare up)

steps.whatToRemember: Whoever last made the fire spread is liable. If the wind did it, no one pays.

phrases.english: If another person came and fanned it, the one who fanned it is liable.
If the wind fanned it, all of them are exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's fire cases from step 27 by adding a third person, or the wind, who fans the flame.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who fans the fire is liable. If the wind fans it, everyone is exempt.

steps.title: A coal is exempt, but a flame makes the giver liable
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש, quoting חזקיה, limits the משנה's exemption for handing fire to a חרש, שוטה, or קטן. It applies only to a coal that the other person fanned. Handing over a flame makes the giver liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said in the name of חזקיה: The משנה only taught this when he handed him a coal and the other person fanned it. But if he handed him a flame, he is liable. Why? His own actions caused the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by going back to the משנה from step 26 and narrowing it. ריש לקיש says the giver is exempt only in one specific kind of case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A coal cannot do much damage until someone fans it. So the חרש, שוטה, or קטן is the one who really started the fire, and the giver is exempt in human court. A flame is already a working fire, so handing it over is itself what causes the damage, and the giver is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this when (a phrase that narrows a ruling)

steps.confusionAlert: 'He is liable' here means the person who handed over the fire, not the חרש, שוטה, or קטן who received it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main dispute of the סוגיא: how much of a fire you have to hand over before you count as the one who caused the damage.

phrases.english: GEMARA
Reish Lakish said in the name of Chizkiya:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁמָּסַר לוֹ גַּחֶלֶת וְלִיבָּהּ,
phrases.english: They only taught this when he handed him a coal and he fanned it,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the משנה from step 26, where someone hands fire to a חרש, שוטה, or קטן and is exempt in human court.

phrases.english: but if he handed him a flame, he is liable.
What is the reason?
His own actions caused it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּחִזְקִיָּה: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא by going back to the משנה in step 26 and limiting where its exemption applies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The exemption applies only to a coal that the receiver fanned. A giver who hands over a flame is liable, because his own act caused the damage.

steps.title: Even a flame is exempt until he hands over branches
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן disagrees. Even handing over a flame leaves the giver exempt, because it was the חרש's handling that caused the fire. The giver becomes liable only when he hands over branches.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Even if he handed him a flame, he is exempt. Why? The tongs of the חרש caused it. And he is not liable until he hands him branches...
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the opposite view to ריש לקיש's. He says the giver is exempt even for a flame, and he starts to describe the case where the giver would be liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יוחנן, a flame by itself still needs someone to bring it to something that will burn. The חרש's handling is what really starts the damage, so the giver is exempt. Only when the giver hands over material that is already set up to burn, like branches, is the damage blamed on him.

keyTerms.meaning: Tongs; here, the חרש's own handling of the fire

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence that ends with גְּווֹזָא continues on the next amud, where the full description of when the giver is liable is given.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Even if he handed him a flame, he is exempt.
What is the reason?
The tongs of the deaf-mute caused it.
phrases.notes: He means that the חרש's own handling of the fire, carrying it over to something that burns, is what caused the damage.

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא מִחַיַּיב עַד שֶׁיִּמְסוֹר לוֹ גְּווֹזָא,
phrases.english: And he is not liable until he hands him branches,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ מָסַר לוֹ שַׁלְהֶבֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to ריש לקיש's statement in step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even handing over a flame leaves the giver exempt. He is liable only when he hands over branches (and the rest of the case continues on the next amud).
